answer: Use the read-only spectrum-monitoring command: show spectrum-monitoring-<name>/<direction>/<center-frequency> [width] [lower-frequency] [upper-frequency] [target-actual-power] [power-actual] [psd-actual]. direction is ingress or egress, default egress, and only egress is currently supported; center-frequency is the band slice centre in MHz, managed by the system. width is the received NMC width in MHz, default 50000. power-actual is the currently received power in dBm, default -99, where -99dBm means the power has not yet been measured by the OCM on the DGE2 card or no power was detected; for egress it is calibrated at the DWDM line port output. psd-actual is the calculated Power Spectral Density in nW/GHz to 2-digit precision, default not-applicable, and does not depend on the spectra width. target-actual-power is the ATPS-calculated target, relevant only when target-power-setting = auto, default -99dBm. Example: show spectrum-monitoring-1-7-dwdm-line2/egress/191968750.

The super-channel object carries a contention-check-status attribute. Values are pending, success, overridden and failk, with default pending. It reports the Contention Check state set via DNA in openwave mode, and it is only applicable if openwave-contention-check is enabled at the super-channel-group level. openwave-contention-check enables the DNA-assisted contention control mechanism in openwave mode; its values are false and true with default false, so contention checking is off unless you turn it on. You can supply contention-check-status on the add: add super-channel-<name> carriers <value> carrier-mode <value> [label] [admin-state] [alarm-report-control] [contention-check-status], and read it back with show super-channel-<name> contention-check-status. The related line-system-mode attribute indicates the L1-to-L0 power control mode on the SCG port and defaults to openwave.

-m is the merge flag. The add command for super-channel-group works in merge mode only: using -m performs a merge, which is a best-effort add. If the target entity does not exist it is created; if it already exists it is updated with any attributes present on the add command, so the command does not fail when the entity is already there. The syntax is: add -m super-channel-group-<name> [label <value>] [admin-state <lock|unlock|maintenance>] [auto-in-service-enabled <value>] [valid-signal-time <value>] [alarm-report-control <allowed|inhibited>] [line-system-mode <value>] [openwave-contention-check <value>]. Defaults: admin-state unlock, alarm-report-control allowed, auto-in-service-enabled false, line-system-mode openwave, valid-signal-time 480 minutes (range 1..7200). Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use show supported-carrier-mode-<name>/<carrier-mode> [capacity] [client-mode] [baud-rate] [application] [compatibility-id] [status] [supported-subtypes], available in Operational and Candidate configuration mode. carrier-mode is an acronymized handle indicating the optical carrier line mode 4-tuple, formatted <Capacity><ClientMode>.<Baud Rate><Application ID>, string length 1..15, for example 600E.84P, 100X.73U or 325M.66P. capacity is the net capacity of the optical carrier in gbps. client-mode is the digital client mode mapped into and transported by the carriers within the superchannel, either ethernet or ethernet-otn. baud-rate is the modulated symbol rate and application is the optical transport application ID the mode is optimized for, string 1..15. compatibility-id identifies carrier modes that can be applied simultaneously, status is the state of the carrier mode, and supported-subtypes is string 0..32, maximum 20 elements.

Use show supported-gain-range-<name>/<gain-range-type> [gain-range-min] [gain-range-max], available in Operational and Candidate configuration mode. gain-range-type is the type of gain range and takes low, high or standard. gain-range-min is the minimum settable gain-target for that range type ('standard'/'low'/'high') and gain-range-max is the maximum settable gain-target for that range type; both are of type gain-value with no default, so the actual numeric limits come from the card being queried rather than from a fixed table. The name key is documented as a flag to enable or disable access control with values true/false, default false.

Different power profiles can be supported to reflect different scenarios when using a card. The user is able to define, per card instance, which profile is in effect, and that choice has an impact on the power estimation for the system. To see what a given card type offers, use show supported-power-profile-<card-type>/<name> [profile-description] [power-draw] [default] in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. card-type is the card type and name is the profile name, both strings. profile-description is a description of the profile, string length 0..255. power-draw is the power draw of the associated equipment when not in low-power, of type decimal64. default is true or false and indicates whether that profile is the default one.

The router ID source is controlled by router-id-mode on the bgp-instance. Its values are use-loopback and manual, and the default is use-loopback, meaning the router ID is taken from the loopback IP unless you set it explicitly. When you choose manual you supply the router-id attribute, an IPv6 or IPv4 address; 0.0.0.0/0 is not supported for IPv4 and 0::0.0 is not supported for IPv6. Syntax: add bgp-instance-<instance-id> local-as <value> [description <value>] [router-id-mode <value>] [router-id <value>], and both fields can be changed later with set bgp-instance-<instance-id>. instance-id is a string of length 1..255 and local-as is a number in the range 1..4294967295. Example: add bgp-instance-10 local-as 24 router-id-mode use-loopback. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

On bgp-neighbor-<instance-id>/<remote-address> the timers are connect-retry-interval, the interval between attempts to establish a session, 1..65535 seconds with default 120; hold-time, the interval a session is considered active without keepalives or other messages, 3..65535 seconds with default 90 and typically set to 3x the keepalive-interval; and keepalive-interval, 1..21845 seconds with default 30, typically 1/3 of the hold-time. The negotiated value is readable as negotiated-hold-time, 0..65535 seconds, default 0. Authentication is available: secure-session selects the authentication method of the session to the peer with values none or TCP-MD5, default none, and password holds the TCP-MD5 authentication key in ASCII format, string 0..80. All of these can be given on add or changed with set.

The routes to be advertised to an external AS must exist in the forwarding table installed by an Interior Gateway Protocol such as OSPF, or by static routes, but not by BGP itself. If the prefix is not present in the IGP tables, you must configure a blackhole static route for it: set the special-next-hop parameter of the static route command to blackhole (special-next-hop takes the value blackhole on both ipv4-static-route and ipv6-static-route). So create the corresponding ipv4-static-route or ipv6-static-route with special-next-hop blackhole alongside your bgp-network entry. The object itself is created with add bgp-network-<instance id>/<remote-address>/<network prefix>, where network-prefix is a decimal 1..64 or 128 and 0.0.0.0/0 and 0::0.0 are not supported as remote-address. A maximum of 100 bgp-network MOs can be configured.

On comm-channel the mtu attribute is the maximum transmission unit size in octets for the physical Ethernet port of the comm channel, and it is available only when the mode is L3. It is a uint16 whose range depends on the platform: 1280..1500 octets on the 1830 GX G30, and 1280..9202 octets on the 1830 GX G40. The default is 1500, and for 1830 GX G40 interface types DCN, AUX, AUX2, OFEC-CC, Craft, CHM6 and UCM4 the default is 1518. mtu can be supplied on add -m comm-channel-<name> or changed with set comm-channel-<name> mtu <value>. Related L3-only attributes are mru, the Maximum-Receive-Unit, 64..1500 octets with default 1500, restart-timer 1..10 seconds default 3, max-failure 2..10 default 5, and peer-address default 0.0.0.0. mode itself takes L1, L2 or L3 and defaults to L3.

LLDP is not running by default. On comm-eth the lldp-admin-status attribute defaults to disabled, meaning the LLDP agent neither transmits nor receives LLDP frames on the port; the other values are tx-only, rx-only and tx-and-rx. It cannot be modified if the mode is L1. Enable it with, for example, set comm-eth-1-5-ETH1 lldp-admin-status tx-and-rx. lldp-transmit-interval is 1..16383 seconds, default 30, and lldp-mgmt-addr-if selects the interface IP advertised as management address; it is empty by default, in which case the loopback IP is used if configured, otherwise the DCN/AUX IP. For speed, auto-negotiation defaults to enabled. duplex-mode (default full), rate (1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000 Mbits or maximum, default maximum) and flow-control (default disabled) are only valid when auto-negotiation is disabled; read back operational-duplex-mode, operational-rate and operational-flow-control.

Use the global dhcp-relay object: set dhcp-relay [mode <value>] [server-address <value>], and show dhcp-relay [mode] [server-address]. mode is the flag indicating the dhcp-relay mode of operation and takes disabled, ipv4 or ipv6, with a default of disabled. server-address holds the DHCP server IP addresses, IPv4 or IPv6; when relay is enabled at least one IP address should be configured. Both parameters are usable with show and set, in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Examples: set dhcp-relay mode ipv4, and set dhcp-relay mode ipv4 server-address 10.220.20.3. Per-interface enabling is done separately with if-dhcp-relay, which obeys these global settings.

Yes. The dns object has an assignment-method attribute that indicates whether the system contains manual and/or dhcp configured values. Its values are manual, dhcp and both, and the default is both, so by default the node accepts DNS servers from DHCP as well as from manual configuration. Syntax: set dns [assignment-method <value>] [enabled <value>] [search <value>] and show dns [assignment-method] [enabled] [search], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. enabled is the flag indicating whether DNS is enabled, true or false, default true. search is the DNS search suffix name, a string of length 0..64 that must contain at least a single dot; set it to an empty string to clear it. Individual servers carry their own origin attribute (dhcp or manual) under dns-server.

Add one with add dns-server-<address> [origin <value>], where address is the IPv4 or IPv6 address of the DNS server. Remove one with delete dns-server-<address>, and inspect with show dns-server-<address> [origin]. The origin attribute is the DNS address assignment method and tells you where the entry came from: dhcp indicates a DNS address that was assigned to this system by a DHCP server, and manual indicates the address was manually configured. The default is manual. You can also convert a DHCP-configured DNS entry into a manually configured one by changing this attribute with set dns-server-<address> origin manual. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add dns-server-10.100.210.243 origin dhcp.

Use the if-dhcp-relay object, which is keyed by interface: set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled <value>], and read it back with show if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled]. if-name is the interface object identifier, a string of length 0..255. dhcp-relay-enabled enables the dhcp-relay function on that interface; it takes true or false and defaults to false. It obeys the global dhcp-relay settings, so the global dhcp-relay mode must be set to ipv4 or ipv6 (it defaults to disabled) and a server-address configured for relaying to work. Access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Example: set if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled true.

By default a new interface is statically addressed and protected. On add interface-<if-name> if-type <value>, ipv4-address-assignment-method and ipv6-address-assignment-method each take static or dhcp and both default to static. ipv4-enabled and ipv6-enabled both default to true, so the interface is connected to both stacks and can send and receive IPv4 and IPv6 packets. protection-mode is the user-given protection mode with values unknown, protected and unprotected, and it defaults to protected; the read-only protection-state reports the current state and defaults to unknown. Other defaults: admin-state unlock (lock, unlock, maintenance), alarm-report-control allowed, proxy-arp-enabled false (only applicable to the DCN interface), and if-dhcp-relay false. if-name is a string 0..64 and if-type is one of ethernet, software-loopback, point-to-point, ppp or hdlc.

Yes, that is what ip-monitoring does. A monitoring instance periodically pings certain destinations and the result takes action on configured static routes. Create it with add ip-monitoring-<name> destination <value> next-hop <value> [probe-interval <value>] [drop-rate <value>] [enabled <value>] [action <value>] [static-route <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>]. action is the action taken when monitoring goes into 'failed' state; it takes none or withdraw and defaults to withdraw. static-route is the list of connected static routes for the instance, maximum 10 elements. next-hop defines the exit interface as an IPv4 or IPv6 source address; the instance is not active until the exit interface is configured. probe-interval is 0..60 seconds, default 5; drop-rate is the accepted ping drop rate in 10% steps, range 1..10, default 1; enabled defaults to true. The route reports monitoring-state as unmonitored, ok or failed.

Use add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>, with show ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> [netmask] [origin] and delete ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip>. There is a stated pre-condition: a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. netmask is the subnet given as a netmask and only valid netmasks are allowed. Three address ranges are disallowed: addresses beginning with 0 (current network), addresses beginning with 127 (loopback), and addresses beginning with 224 through 255 (broadcast, multicast and experimental). The read-only origin shows the assignment method, static, dhcp or auto-config, default static. To list available interfaces, type ? after ipv4-address-. Examples: add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask '255.255.240.0' and add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0.

On ipv4-static-route the distance attribute is the distance to the next hop, a number in the range 1..255, and it defaults to 1. A discard route is created with special-next-hop, whose value is blackhole (also its listed default). Blackhole static routes are needed because routes advertised to an external AS must exist in the forwarding table installed by an IGP such as OSPF or by static routes, not by BGP itself; for prefixes not present in the IGP tables you configure a blackhole static route. Syntax: add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>]. advertised defaults to false; set true and the route is advertised in the routing protocol, and for OSPF as an AS external route if OSPF is configured as an ASBR. origin is manual or dhcp, default manual.

It is the same shape but the subnet is given as a prefix length rather than a netmask: add ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> prefix-length <value>, with show ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> [prefix-length] [origin] and delete ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip>. prefix-length is the length of the subnet prefix, a number in the range 1..128, and only valid prefixes are allowed to be configured. Note that an IPv6 /127 subnet is currently supported on unprotected DCN-A (DCN) interfaces and does not apply to broadcast links with larger subnets. if-name is the interface object identifier, string 0..64. The read-only origin gives the assignment method, static, dhcp or auto-config, default static. Type ? after ipv6-address- to list the available interfaces. Examples: add ipv6-address-1-AUX-1/AAAA::186 prefix-length 10 and add ipv6-address-DCN-B/2620:38:4001:192:10:220:192:213 prefix-length 64.

Yes. Static routes can be added with the DCN-B interface when DCN is operating in active-active mode. Use add ipv6-static-route-<ipv6-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>] and name DCN-B in the interface parameter. The VRF bound to that interface needs to match the vrf given on the static route. Example: add ipv6-static-route-2620:38:4::/64/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN-B. Defaults on the route: distance 1 (range 1..255), advertised false, origin manual (or dhcp), special-next-hop blackhole, label a string 0..256. Access is Operational and Candidate configuration mode.

Use show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. There may be multiple management addresses configured on the remote system identified by a particular index whose information is received on the local system, and each must have a distinct management address type (subtype) and management address (address). lldp-port is the local port connected to this LLDP neighbor, direction is ingress or egress, and address is the string used to contact the management entity, length 0..64. if-subtype is unknown, if-index or system-port-number; if-id is the interface number; address-oid is the OID identifying the hardware component or protocol entity associated with the advertised management address, string 0..128.

They carry the same attribute set but differ in key and in which side's addresses they show. management-address is keyed show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> and includes a direction key of ingress or egress; it covers the management addresses received on the local system for the remote system on that LLDP port. management-address-local is keyed show management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address>, with no direction key, and shows the management address information from the local LLDP ports, that is what this node advertises. Both expose if-subtype (unknown, if-index, system-port-number), if-id and address-oid (string 0..128), and both run in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. For management-address-local the guide notes address-oid is currently an empty string. Example: show management-address-local.

Yes, that is the use-as-source attribute on the networking object. It names the interface to use as the source address and takes a string of length 0..64, with no default stated. Set it with set networking [use-as-source <value>] and read it back with show networking [use-as-source]. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: set networking use-as-source LO-MGMT, and show networking to view the current networking information. use-as-source is the only parameter on this command.

Use show networking-services. It shows the list of network services and takes no parameters at all: the syntax is simply show networking-services, with no keys or optional attribute filters. It runs in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. It is a show-only command; there is no set or add form. For the source-address setting and other networking information, use the separate networking command (show networking / set networking use-as-source).
